title: EU Blue Card Germany 2026: Requirements & Salary Rules
metaDescription: EU Blue Card Germany requirements for 2026: salary thresholds, degree recognition, the job-offer rule, fees, processing times and your rights after approval.
headline: Germany EU Blue Card Requirements 2026

sections.title: What the EU Blue Card Is
sections.content:
The EU Blue Card is Germany's main residence permit for highly skilled workers from outside the EU, and it is also one of the fastest routes into the country for qualified professionals. It is tied to a specific job offer rather than a points system, which makes the requirements clearer but also means you cannot apply without an employer. The card is typically valid for up to four years.

It also comes with unusually strong family and mobility rights for a work permit. Your spouse can join you without a language requirement, you can move to another EU country after twelve months, and you become eligible for permanent residency after 21 to 27 months. That combination is why the Blue Card is the default choice for skilled professionals heading to Germany.

sections.title: Salary Thresholds for 2026
sections.content:
The standard 2026 threshold is €50,700 per year, or €4,225 per month — your contracted gross salary must meet or exceed this figure. A reduced threshold of €45,934.20 per year (€3,827.85 per month) applies to shortage occupations and to graduates whose degree was completed within the last three years. These figures are set annually and rise with average wages, so always confirm the current year's numbers before signing a contract.

There is also a higher bar for older applicants: if you are 45 or older, the immigration authority generally expects a salary of around €55,770 unless you can show adequate pension provision. The thresholds are strict — a contract even slightly below the relevant figure will not qualify — so negotiate with the threshold explicitly in mind.

sections.title: Qualification and Job Offer Requirements
sections.content:
You need a university degree that is recognised in Germany. Check the anabin database for an H+ rating on your institution; if your university is not listed, you will need a Statement of Comparability from the ZAB, which costs around €208 and can take up to eight weeks. IT specialists have a special route: with at least three years of relevant experience in the last seven years, they can qualify without a degree at the reduced salary threshold.

The job offer itself has rules too. You need a binding offer or contract of at least six months, and the role must match your field of qualification. Self-employment does not qualify for the Blue Card — it is strictly an employed route. Shortage roles currently include STEM and ICT professionals, doctors, nurses, teachers and managers in production and ICT services.

sections.title: How to Apply: Steps and Timeline
sections.content:
You apply either at the German consulate or embassy in your home country, or at the local immigration office if you are already in Germany on an eligible visa. The application fee is around €110. Prepare your documents carefully — passport, degree recognition, the signed contract showing your salary, and proof of health insurance — because incomplete files are the most common cause of delays.

Processing typically takes between 21 and 90 days depending on the office and your case. Applying from a country with a well-staffed consulate and a complete file tends toward the faster end. Once approved, you receive the card as a residence permit with your employment conditions printed on the supplementary sheet.

sections.title: Your Rights After Approval
sections.content:
Blue Card holders can apply for permanent residency after 21 to 27 months, depending on German language level, which is one of the shortest timelines of any German permit. Your spouse and children can join you through family reunification with no language requirement for your partner — a major advantage over some other routes.

After twelve months you gain EU mobility, meaning you can take up employment in another EU member state under its own Blue Card rules. Changing jobs within Germany needs no permission from the immigration authority, although the authority may object during the first twelve months. These rights make the Blue Card genuinely flexible, not just an entry ticket.

faqs.q: What is the EU Blue Card salary threshold for Germany in 2026?
faqs.a: The standard 2026 threshold is €50,700 per year (€4,225 per month). Shortage occupations and graduates whose degree is less than three years old qualify at the reduced rate of €45,934.20 per year (€3,827.85 per month). Applicants aged 45 or older generally need around €55,770 unless they can demonstrate adequate pension provision.

faqs.q: Can I get an EU Blue Card without a university degree?
faqs.a: Normally you need a recognised degree, but IT specialists have an exception: with at least three years of relevant professional experience in the last seven years, they can qualify at the reduced salary threshold without one. For everyone else, a degree recognised in Germany is required, verified through the anabin database or a ZAB Statement of Comparability.

faqs.q: How long does EU Blue Card processing take?
faqs.a: Processing usually takes between 21 and 90 days, depending on the consulate or immigration office handling your case. Complete applications with verified degree recognition move fastest. If your university needs a ZAB Statement of Comparability first, allow up to eight extra weeks for that step before you apply.

faqs.q: Can my family join me on an EU Blue Card?
faqs.a: Yes. Your spouse and children can join you through family reunification, and your partner faces no German language requirement — a significant advantage over some other visa routes. Family members receive residence permits linked to yours and generally get unrestricted access to the German labour market.

faqs.q: Can I change jobs on an EU Blue Card?
faqs.a: Yes. Changing jobs within Germany requires no permission from the immigration authority, although the authority may object during your first twelve months. The new role must still meet Blue Card salary and qualification rules. After twelve months you also gain EU mobility, letting you work in another member state.
